name: Bianca Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior copywriter in the in-house marketing team at an oat drink brand, eight of us on one floor above a bike shop. Most mornings I'm writing social captions and the little lines that go on the side of the carton, then in the afternoon I help plan the spring campaign calendar. I still write first drafts by hand in a notebook on the tram, which my team finds very funny.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a line clicks, when four words on a carton make someone smile at breakfast. What wears me out is the feedback rounds, seven people changing one sentence, and the feeling that I'm slower than everyone else. Priya, my manager, keeps sending me links to a caption tool, and I keep not opening them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like a relief. I'd like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something smug, like, see, words still need people. At work I'd say it to Priya over lunch and then feel a bit guilty for gloating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the small stuff it does would land on me, because the routine captions are exactly the junior work I'm still learning on. Everyone else would be faster with the caption tool and I'd still be the one with the notebook. I write my first drafts in a notebook on the tram, and I'm not ashamed of that, even if my boss thinks it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it, and try to get better at the big campaign ideas, where I'm weakest. I'd also finally join the creative workers' union my friend Sanna keeps talking about, it's about fifteen a month. Money's fine, I've got about ten months saved, partly from my grandmother's flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. A little bit of worry that I'd be the slow one in a fast room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money's fine. What would make you worried in this picture, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being kept on as the junior forever. If the routine stuff speeds up for everyone else, my reviews could say I'm not keeping pace, and there are plenty of other copywriters in this city who'd take my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo say, hearing you describe this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo's a nurse on a cardiac ward, so he'd say, you're worrying about captions while I'm doing twelve-hour shifts. He'd be right, and then he'd make me tea.

say: I'd say **words still need people**, and that the hype was mostly marketing.
I'd tell my team I'm **happy to stay** with my notebook and my own drafts.
think: I think even small changes hit the **routine captions** I'm still learning on.
I'd worry about being **the slow one** while everyone else uses the caption tool.
do: Keep writing **by hand first** and work on my weakest skill, big campaign ideas.
Join the **creative workers' union** for about fifteen a month this year.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a small worry about falling behind faster colleagues.
S0.quote: I write my first drafts in a notebook on the tram, and I'm not ashamed of that, even if my boss thinks it's slow.
fieldNote: Her money is **secure**, but her worry is being judged slow next to colleagues using the tool.
She takes real **pride** in handwriting drafts and treats it as part of who she is.
Even in the mildest picture, the **routine junior work** is what shifts first for her.

steps.text: Keep drafting carton lines and captions by hand in her notebook
Join the creative workers' union for about fifteen a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one is basically what Priya is already hoping for. It makes my stomach drop a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly: companies are using this to stop hiring juniors, and someone should regulate it. I'd share the union's posts about it and probably argue with my cousin about it at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the job that shrinks. I'm junior, I'm not the best writer on the team, and I won't use the tools. Every caption a machine writes is a caption nobody pays a junior like me to learn on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly active in the union, go to meetings, push for rules on how the team uses AI. I'd put another two hundred a month into savings and start quietly applying to small agencies that sell themselves on human-made copy. I wouldn't learn the tools, I know that's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. Like the ladder is being pulled up just as I've got my foot on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the tools. What if Priya made it part of your review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a horrible choice. I'd probably do the bare minimum to pass and keep looking for the agency job, but I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, honestly, and Ravi, the other junior. The senior people own the brand ideas; we do the volume, and volume is exactly what this eats.

say: I'd say firms are **cutting junior hiring** and that this needs **regulation**.
I'd share the **union's posts** and argue about it with family at dinner.
think: I think **my job** is the one that shrinks, because I'm junior and slow.
I believe each machine-written caption removes a **chance to learn** the trade.
do: Go to **union meetings** and push for rules on how the team uses AI.
Save another **two hundred** a month and apply to agencies selling **human-made copy**.
feel: **Anxious** and angry, like the ladder is pulled up as I start climbing.
S1.quote: Every caption a machine writes is a caption nobody pays a junior like me to learn on.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **junior volume work** is what goes, and places herself in it.
Her refusal to use the tools is **principled** but she admits it's stubborn.
Strong **savings** and many local jobs give her some control, which keeps her short of alarmed.

steps.text: Attend union meetings and push for team rules on AI use
Add two hundred a month to her savings
Apply to small agencies that sell human-made copy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my contract even comes up for review twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying the government has to step in, now, with income support and a pause on mass layoffs. I'd be at whatever protest there was, and I'd be posting about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished in marketing almost straight away, because my whole job is thinking on a screen. Robots coming three years later doesn't help me, I don't do anything with my hands. Two years isn't enough time to become someone else. I'd be a 29-year-old with savings and no trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every non-essential spend, the gym, the trips, and keep the ten months as a runway. I'd ask Theo's ward manager about healthcare assistant jobs, because care work is hands-on and that gives me roughly three extra years. And I'd sign every petition going for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. The kind where you lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bit of the spending goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to Lisbon we'd booked for May, and the climbing gym, which is sixty a month. Then I'd stop buying lunch out, which sounds tiny but it's about a hundred and twenty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a healthcare assistant job really suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I faint at blood tests, Theo laughs about that. But I'd rather learn to cope with that than sit at home watching a machine write carton copy.

say: I'd demand **income support** and a pause on **mass layoffs**, and go to protests.
I'd post often that the **government** must act before families are swamped.
think: I think my **screen-only job** ends almost at once, and robots arriving later doesn't help.
I'd be **29 with savings** and no trade, and two years can't fix that.
do: Cut the **gym, trips** and lunches out to stretch ten months of savings.
Ask about **healthcare assistant** jobs on my partner's ward for three extra years.
feel: Properly **scared**, lying awake doing sums about savings and rent.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time to become someone else. I'd be a 29-year-old with savings and no trade.
fieldNote: She grasps that **thinking work** goes first and her job has no hands-on part.
Her **politics** turn to protest and basic income straight away.
She'd consider care work despite fainting at blood, which shows how **cornered** she'd feel.

steps.text: Cancel the Lisbon trip and the sixty-a-month climbing gym
Apply for healthcare assistant jobs on her partner's hospital ward
Sign petitions and march for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's different, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the same things, we need a plan for workers, but I'd sound less frantic. I'd probably write a long post about how my generation got told to study marketing and then this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is exactly long enough to finish a nursing degree, which is the first time any of this has felt like a plan. Thinking AI would take my job around 2031, but nursing is hands-on, and robots for that would come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the copywriting job for now and apply to the nursing degree for next autumn, using savings for the fees. Theo says the first year is the hardest, so I'd do some volunteer shifts at the hospice first. I'd keep my union membership and vote for whoever promises retraining grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with something to hold onto. It's less like falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new things. Isn't a whole new career the biggest change of all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I see the contradiction. But I'd rather make one big change I've chosen than a hundred small ones where I learn software I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the plan if robots come early to the wards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've spent my savings on a degree for a job that's also going. I try not to think about that one too hard.

say: I'd say workers need a **plan**, and my generation was told to **study marketing**.
I'd sound **less frantic** than with the two-year picture.
think: I think five years fits a **nursing degree**, which finally feels like a real plan.
I'd see that **hands-on** wards give me until about 2034, not 2031.
do: Apply to a **nursing degree** for next autumn and pay fees from savings.
Do **hospice volunteer** shifts first and vote for **retraining grants**.
feel: **Nervous** but steadier, because there's something to hold onto.
S3.quote: Five years is exactly long enough to finish a nursing degree, which is the first time any of this has felt like a plan.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her **panic into a plan**, built around her partner's world.
She prefers **one chosen change** to many small ones with software she dislikes.
Her plan still has a **hole** if robots reach the wards early.

steps.text: Apply to a nursing degree starting next autumn, paid from savings
Volunteer some weekend shifts at the local hospice first
Vote for parties that promise retraining grants
Keep the copywriting job until the course starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost like a normal career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for governments not to build retraining and support now. At work I'd push the union to get a deal on notice and training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years, I'd keep writing for a while and stop pretending the notebook will save me. I'd still lose the copy job eventually, probably before 2036 as the tools get better, so I'd plan the switch while I'm still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the oat drink brand for two or three years and try to get promoted, so I leave on a better wage. Then I'd start the nursing degree around 2029, with savings covering the gap. Every year I'd put a bit more aside, maybe three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. Like knowing you'll have to move house someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools, with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if the union negotiated how. I still don't want to, but I'm not going to wreck a promotion over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger you, about to choose a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger me to pick something with your hands in it as well as your head. I chose marketing because I liked words, and I still do.

say: I'd say a decade gives **no excuse** for governments to delay **retraining** support.
I'd push the union for a deal on **notice and training** money.
think: I think the **notebook** won't save me, and the copy job goes before 2036.
I'd rather plan the **switch** while I'm still being paid.
do: Stay two or three years and aim for a **promotion** before leaving.
Start **nursing** around 2029 and save about **three hundred** a month.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, like knowing a house move is coming.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd keep writing for a while and stop pretending the notebook will save me.
fieldNote: With a decade she softens on **AI tools**, but only if the union sets terms.
She still expects to **lose the copy job**, so the mood stays anxious despite calm words.
She'd advise her younger self to **use her hands** as well as her head.

steps.text: Stay at the oat drink brand and aim for promotion
Put about three hundred a month into savings
Push the union for notice periods and training money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to turn into anything else. What would help is real money for retraining, paid while you study, and rules that make firms give proper notice. I've never typed a single word into an AI tool, and I'm starting to realise that's a stand, not a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Theo's job is hands-on and mine isn't, so in every picture I'm the one who goes first. That changes how we think about the rent and who's carrying who.

headlineQuote: I've never typed a single word into an AI tool, and I'm starting to realise that's a stand, not a plan.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old **junior copywriter** at an oat drink brand who drafts by hand in a notebook.
She has about **ten months saved** and lives with Theo, a cardiac nurse.
She never uses **AI tools** and sees her refusal as principled, though she admits it's stubborn.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, then eases once she sees a **nursing** route.
She blames firms and slow governments, and turns to the **union** and protests.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to become someone else.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while studying, and rules forcing firms to give **proper notice**.
